newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma slams Amnesty rights abuse report.
newsitem.headline: Burma slams Amnesty rights abuse report.

text.p: Burma's military government on Wednesday dismissed Amnesty International's scathing report on its human rights record as "ridiculous", and said it was propoganda for anti-Burmese organisations.
"We the people of Myanmar (Burma) are amazed at the increasing intensity of ridiculous allegations Amnesty International comes up with each year," a government spokesman told Reuters.
"It is also regretful to learn that such a reputable organisation becomes a press office or a propaganda machine for the anti-Myanmar Government organisations," he said.
The Amnesty report said political repression and human rights violations in Burma last year reached their highest levels since the violent state suppression of a popular uprising in late 1988.
The human rights body said more than 2,000 people were arrested in 1996 for calling for human rights reform, and that opposition party members were attacked by organised mobs.
Amnesty also urged the international community to redouble the pressure on the Burmese authorities to improve their human rights record.
Some major Western multinational companies such as PepsiCo and Liz Claiborne have already stopped doing business in Burma under pressure from their shareholders.

"Those governments with influence, particularly the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) gathering in Singapore this week, need to think again about how to pressure the Burmese authorities to improve their human rights record," Amnesty said.
Seven-member ASEAN, which says constructive engagement will bring about reforms in Burma, has agreed to admit it as a member along with Laos and Cambodia some time in the future.
Amnesty also accused the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) of "an almost complete intolerance of any peaceful political activity whatsoever".
Pro-democracy opposition leader Aung Sun Kyi was repeatedly refused permission to leave her compound in 1996 after having been freed from six years of house arrest in July 1995, it said.
The government spokesman said Amnesty was "extremely ignorant of the true situation" in Burma or had other interests in the country.
"There is a Myanmar proverb - it is more difficult to try to wake up a person who is pretending to be asleep," he added.
